title: Your First ASP Application
subtopics: Running an ASP page through IIS
Verifying the generated HTML in a browser
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of your first asp application in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Creating an .asp file and Writing a basic server-side script.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study your first asp application as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 8 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: Your First ASP Application matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Classic ASP is a server-side page technology: IIS processes an `.asp` request, executes server-side script, and returns the resulting response. For 'Your First ASP Application', keep a clear boundary between what runs on the server and what the browser receives. The curriculum places this topic in the foundations stage, so the aim is to recognize the role, context, and limits before building larger workflows.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Creating an .asp file; Writing a basic server-side script; Combining HTML and VBScript; Running an ASP page through IIS; Verifying the generated HTML in a browser. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Your First ASP Application
content_blocks.code:
<%@ Language="VBScript" %> <% Option Explicit Dim visitorName visitorName = "Learner" %>

Hello, <%= Server.HTMLEncode(visitorName) %>

Server date: <%= Server.HTMLEncode(CStr(Date)) %>
content_blocks.expected_output: A greeting and server-generated date appear in HTML.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run through a local IIS website with the Classic ASP feature enabled. `Server.HTMLEncode` keeps dynamic values from being interpreted as markup. The standard CodeLeaf browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute Classic ASP, VBScript, ADO, IIS commands, PowerShell, or SQL. This block is therefore marked for static inspection unless you run it in the clearly identified local tool.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original sample and test data. Change one condition, input, provider setting, or runtime option at a time, then compare observed behavior with the expected result.
content_blocks.limitations: Not executed during course generation. Classic ASP examples require a configured Windows/IIS environment with the matching ASP scripting engine and any required COM/ADO providers. Provider-specific and IIS-version-specific behavior must be verified locally.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Run the example only on a local or test IIS site with the Classic ASP feature enabled. Record the OS, IIS version, site binding, physical directory, and the exact URL used. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of your first asp application. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small, reviewable demonstration of your first asp application using synthetic data. Include at least one of these syllabus concepts: Creating an .asp file. State the expected result first, then add one invalid or boundary case and explain how your program should behave.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

summary: Your First ASP Application is one step in the larger Classic ASP request, state, data, security, or maintenance workflow.
The syllabus coverage includes Creating an .asp file; Writing a basic server-side script; Combining HTML and VBScript; Running an ASP page through IIS; Verifying the generated HTML in a browser.
A reproducible legacy-code example records input, environment/version, expected outcome, observed outcome, and a meaningful failure case.
expected_output: A greeting and server-generated date appear in HTML.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
